# Creamy Italian Risotto

## The Right Rice

Risotto requires short-grain, high-starch Italian rice varieties such as Arborio, Carnaroli,
or Vialone Nano. These cultivars contain high levels of amylopectin starch that dissolves
into the cooking liquid to create the characteristic creamy consistency without adding cream.
Carnaroli holds its shape best and is preferred by professional cooks.

## Building the Base

Soften finely diced shallots or onion in butter and a splash of white wine over medium heat.
Toast the dry rice grains in the fat for two minutes until they become slightly translucent
around the edges. Add white wine and stir until absorbed before adding stock.

## The Ladling Technique

Add hot stock one ladle at a time, stirring constantly and waiting for each addition to be
absorbed before adding the next. The constant agitation releases starch from the rice and
creates the creamy texture. Use warm stock to maintain temperature; cold stock would shock
the rice and slow cooking unevenly. This process takes 18 to 22 minutes total.

## Mantecatura

The final step is mantecatura: remove the pan from heat and vigorously stir in cold butter
cut into cubes and freshly grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese. The violent stirring emulsifies
the butter into the starchy liquid, creating a luxurious, glossy, creamy sauce that coats each
grain. Serve immediately on warm plates as the risotto continues to thicken as it cools.

## Classic Variations

Risotto alla Milanese uses saffron and bone marrow for a golden hue. Risotto al funghi uses
dried porcini and fresh mushrooms. Seafood risotto omits cheese in the traditional southern
Italian style and finishes with olive oil instead of butter.
